 Current Sunscreen Users Are More Likely to Teach Children Sun Protection
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 Active sunscreen users are significantly more likely to educate their children about the importance of sun protection compared to nonusers, according to research published as a short report in Archives of Dermatological Research. 
 To explore these relationships, the research team focused on a unique population based in Miami, evaluating the sociodemographic variables that shape sunscreen habits. The authors noted that sunscreen use patterns frequently vary according to cultural perceptions, race, ethnicity, and access to healthcare. The primary objective was to clarify how specific demographic determinants influence compliance and to identify opportunities for dermatologists to enhance patient adherence.
 The survey findings revealed a substantial contrast between the proportion of participants who educate their children about sun safety and those who received similar guidance in their youth. While 85 percent of respondents reported actively educating their children about the importance of sunscreen, only 42 percent reported having received sunscreen education from their own parents. Personal usage habits emerged as a powerful correlate of parental instruction: individuals who actively used sunscreen were significantly more likely to educate their children regarding sun protection than nonusers, yielding a highly significant statistical relationship (p = 0.0009).
 When the researchers tested whether an individual’s own childhood exposure to parental sunscreen guidance influenced their likelihood of educating their offspring, they found no statistically significant relationship (p = 0.692). This lack of association indicates that an individual’s recollection of parental instruction does not dictate whether they provide photoprotection guidance to their children. 
 Sociodemographic evaluations within the Miami cohort revealed notable cultural and generational distinctions in childhood education. Hispanic and Latino participants were significantly more likely to report having received sunscreen education from their parents compared to their non-Hispanic and non-Latino peers, a difference supported by chi-square analysis (chi-square = 8.19 with 1 degree of freedom, N = 132, p = 0.004). Generational changes were also evident across age demographics, as younger participants were significantly more likely than older respondents to report receiving sunscreen education during childhood (p = 0.019).
 The investigation also evaluated consumer preferences regarding specific sunscreen formulations, uncovering distinct differences based on gender and age. Among the 99 participants evaluated for formulation preferences, female respondents exhibited a significantly higher preference for tinted sunscreen compared to male respondents (chi-square = 4.61 with 1 degree of freedom, N = 99, p = 0.032). Preference for tinted formulations also varied across age brackets, with younger participants demonstrating a significantly greater likelihood of choosing tinted sunscreen products compared to older participants (p = 0.047).
 In their conclusion, the study authors highlighted that a patient’s recollected upbringing predicts very little about their current sun-protective behavior, indicating that current health practices are independent and directly modifiable. Citing established evidence that counseling delivered by dermatologists effectively increases sun-protective behaviors, the researchers underscored a key opportunity for clinical practice. By reinforcing sunscreen adherence during patient visits, dermatologists can modify current patient habits and, in doing so, positively influence the photoprotective education delivered to future generations.
 Subject of Research: Intergenerational sunscreen education and sociodemographic factors influencing sun protection habits
 Article Title: Sunscreen education: an analysis of intergenerational sunscreen education and sociodemographic factors that shape sunscreen habits
 Article References: Hartoyo, M., Pulumati, A., Kim, S., Cooke, R., Junco, V., Dawes, D. M., & Nouri, K. (2026). Sunscreen education: an analysis of intergenerational sunscreen education and sociodemographic factors that shape sunscreen habits. Archives of Dermatological Research, 318 (1), Article 560. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00403-026-04929-5
